record.original_question: If p is k-avoidable, then there are arbitrary long circular words on k letters that avoid p.

evidence.quote: If p is k-avoidable, then there are arbitrary long circular words on k letters that avoid p.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $A_k=\{0,1,\dots,k-1\}$ be a $k$-letter alphabet, and let $E$ be a separate alphabet of "pattern variables." A pattern is a word $p\in E^+$. A word $w\in A_k^*$ is said to encounter $p$ if there exists a non-erasing morphism $h:E^+\to A_k^+$ such that $h(p)$ is a factor of $w$; otherwise $w$ avoids $p$. A circular word of length $n$ on $A_k$ is an equivalence class of $A_k^n$ under cyclic rotation; its factors are all the factors (of every length) of the linear word $ww$ that have length at most $n$. A circular word avoids $p$ if none of its factors encounters $p$. The pattern $p$ is called $k$-avoidable if there exist infinitely many (equivalently, arbitrarily long) linear words over $A_k$ that avoid $p$.

Prove or disprove: for every pattern $p$, if $p$ is $k$-avoidable, then there exist arbitrarily long circular words on $k$ letters that avoid $p$.
artifact.status_search_result: The statement appears as a conjecture in the compilation of open problems from the WORDS conference series (listed as Conjecture 1.1.03.7). No published resolution was found in a web search; related conjectures about circular words avoiding patterns remain open.

status_evidence.snippet: Studies circular words avoiding patterns; partial results are known but the general conjecture relating k-avoidability to existence of arbitrarily long circular avoiding words is not resolved.
